FreeEvolve: Learning to Evolve Beyond Fixed Loops

Lecheng Kong ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Email: jkong@amazon.com    Like Hui11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Email: likehui@amazon.com    Nikos Kanakaris Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Email: nikosk@amazon.com    Prithwish Jana ††thanks: Work done as an intern at AWS AI Labs. Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: pjana7@gatech.edu    Sahika Genc Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Email: sahika@amazon.com    Narayanan Sadagopan Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Email: sdgpn@amazon.com
Abstract

Agent evolvers automate the design of the prompts, skills and workflows around language model agents, yet the optimization process they follow is still designed by hand: a fixed search loop decides how candidates are evaluated, which are kept and when the search stops. We propose FreeEvolve, which automates this process as well. An environment specifies the goal, target agent, evaluator, data and resource limits; within these limits, the evolver itself decides what to test, how much evidence to collect, which candidates to pursue and when to stop. These decisions follow an editable evolution skill, which we improve through meta-evolution by scoring each candidate skill on the fresh target agent it produces. The optimization process thus becomes a capability learned from experience rather than a loop engineered in advance. On τ3\tau^{3}-bench, ARC-AGI-2, ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench 2.1, FreeEvolve controls the evolution campaign by itself, yet improves the primary held-out metric by 13.6 points on average and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers. The learned process keeps improving with experience: meta-evolved skills add 6.96.9 points over the seed skill on fresh target agents, demonstrating transferability across environments.

Project page w/ interactive demo: https://freeevolve.github.io/

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to solve a wide range of tasks through reasoning and tool use. However, for a frozen LLM, the performance of an agent depends heavily on the harness around it. The harness determines how the model reasons, acts and recovers from failures. Therefore, improving the harness can improve agent performance without changing the model weights. Recent studies have started to automate this process by treating prompts, skills and agent workflows as editable components (Karten et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c). Following this direction, we focus on agent evolvers. An evolver executes a target agent, examines its failures and modifies its harness based on the collected evidence.

Although evolvers automate the design of agent harnesses, the optimization process they follow is still designed by hand. Before evolution begins, a human-designed search loop fixes which tasks are evaluated, how often measurements are repeated, how candidates are compared and when the search stops. On one hand this requires extensive design expertise. On the other hand, a loop encodes assumptions about evaluation noise, task difficulty, useful curricula and available parallelism. These assumptions vary across agents and environments and can change as evidence arrives, yet an evolver that only proposes edits cannot act on that evidence, and adapting the loop means re-engineering it by hand. We therefore ask: Can the optimization process itself be automated, so that the evolver organizes its own improvement campaign and learns how to do so from experience?

To this end, we propose FreeEvolve, a framework that automates the optimization process of agent evolution. The main idea is to treat campaign organization as a capability that the evolver exercises and learns, rather than a loop that humans design. Our framework separates the improvement problem from the procedure used to solve it. A bounded environment defines the goal, editable target, available data and resource constraints. The evolver is invoked once and remains in control until it returns an improved target. After each environment execution, it uses the collected evidence to decide what to do next. This control allows the evolver to adapt the campaign without following an evolution loop defined in advance.

Automating the process: campaign autonomy. Campaign autonomy allows the improvement process to adapt as new evidence becomes available. During evolution, the evolver can focus on tasks with frequent failures before validating more broadly. It can repeat uncertain comparisons, explore different candidates and reallocate resources based on the observed results. It can also stop when additional evidence is unlikely to change the best candidate. These decisions are made as evolution unfolds instead of being fixed in advance by a predefined search loop.

Learning the process: meta-evolution. Campaign autonomy alone does not guarantee an effective improvement process. The evolver still needs guidance on how to use this control. To address this issue, we represent the campaign policy as an editable evolution skill. We then improve this skill through meta-evolution. Each candidate skill is used to run complete improvement campaigns in target-agent environments. The resulting agents and campaign traces are used to evaluate and refine the skill. Meta-evolution therefore produces a self-contained evolution skill that can be applied unchanged to new environments without retaining the original agents or execution artifacts.

Experimental results. We evaluate FreeEvolve on τ3\tau^{3}-bench (Shi et al., 2026), ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet et al., 2026), ARC-AGI-3, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026). Without any hand-designed loop, meta-evolution raises held-out mean performance from 33.3%33.3\% to 51.7%51.7\%, 55.4%55.4\% to 69.1%69.1\%, 61.0%61.0\% to 81.6%81.6\%, and 80.9%80.9\% to 82.5%82.5\%, respectively, matching or exceeding hand-designed evolvers on six of seven metrics. The automated process is also learnable and reusable. Installed on a fresh worker, the frozen meta-evolved skill outperforms the seed skill on all four mean metrics and all three available pass@3 metrics, and improves over a no-data LLM rewrite in all four environments, so execution experience, not instruction rewriting alone, drives the gain. A skill meta-evolved on τ3\tau^{3}-bench also reaches 64.3%64.3\% mean accuracy on ARC-AGI-2 and 71.0%71.0\% Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) on ARC-AGI-3, matching or exceeding the skills meta-evolved directly on those environments.

Contributions.

  • •

    Automating the optimization process. Conceptually, we identify the hand-designed search loop as the remaining manual component of agent evolution and recast it as a campaign policy that the evolver executes and that can be learned from improvement experience.

  • •

    Campaign autonomy and meta-evolution. Technically, a bounded environment gives the evolver control of campaign decisions, while a self-contained evolution skill makes that control improvable through meta-evolution. Candidate skills are evaluated through the worker campaigns they organize.

  • •

    A learnable and reusable process. Empirically, without a hand-designed loop, FreeEvolve matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers on six of seven held-out metrics across four environments. Meta-evolution improves the process itself, which then transfers across environments, yields workers that transfer to cheaper models, reaches a stronger skill with fewer tokens, and benefits from more capable evolver models.

2 Related Work

Automating harness design. Recent systems automate the design of the prompts, skills, code, and workflows around a fixed language model (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Karten et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Lou et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), and evolutionary coding systems improve programs and agent harnesses through model-generated edits (Sharma, 2025; Novikov et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026). They automate what is edited; the search process that decides what to evaluate, which candidates to keep, and when to stop is typically specified in advance by the system designer.

Automating the improver. Meta-evolution and self-improvement make the improvement mechanism itself editable, evolving mutation prompts, program improvers, self-editing agents, search strategies, context-producing skills, or meta-agents (Fernando et al., 2024; Zelikman et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025; Qu and Lu, 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b; Srikanth et al., 2026). Meta-Harness, does not do meta-evolution, it lets a coding proposer read candidate code, scores, and traces before editing (Lee et al., 2026). HyperAgents, like FreeEvolve, evolves at the meta level, jointly evolving task agents and the meta-agents that improve them, so its procedure can change across outer iterations (Zhang et al., 2026b). These prior work focus on improving a fixed campaign.

Automating the improvement process. FreeEvolve extends automation to the process within a run: the evolver organizes its own campaign as results arrive, and meta-evolution learns the skill that guides it from completed campaigns. What is learned is neither a better artifact nor a search procedure for the next run, but a reusable way of running improvement campaigns. Appendix E discusses broader related work.

3 Method

In this section, we present the proposed FreeEvolve framework. Campaign autonomy changes who organizes the evolution process. In a conventional search loop, the framework invokes an evolver or proposer at predefined stages and retains control over evaluation, candidate selection and stopping. In FreeEvolve, the evolver is invoked once and remains in control until it returns an improved target. Briefly, the framework operates at two connected levels, as illustrated in Figure 2. At the agent level, a bounded environment defines the improvement goal, editable target, available data and resource constraints. The evolver follows an evolution skill and organizes the complete improvement campaign. It decides what to evaluate, how to allocate resources and when to stop. At the meta level, the evolution skill becomes the editable target. The meta-evolver evaluates candidate skills through complete agent-level campaigns and uses the collected evidence to improve the skill. Both levels use the same environment interface and evolution operation.

3.1 A Bounded Interface for Campaign Autonomy

Giving control to the evolver requires a well-defined problem boundary. Within this boundary, the evolver can explore the problem in different ways. However, it cannot change the goal, evaluation rules or resource limits. We define an environment initialized with target x0x_{0} as

ℰ⁡[x0]=(g,𝒟,x0,Rℰ,𝒞ℰ),\mathcal{E}[x_{0}]=\left(g,\mathcal{D},x_{0},R_{\mathcal{E}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{E}}\right), (1)

where gg is the improvement goal, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the available data and x0x_{0} is the initial editable target. The execution function RℰR_{\mathcal{E}} runs a candidate target xx under an execution request uu and returns an artifact bundle aa:

a=Rℰ​(x,u).a=R_{\mathcal{E}}(x,u). (2)

The evolver chooses uu, and 𝒞ℰ\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{E}} defines which requests are valid. The execution function determines which interactions are possible; it does not prescribe when or in what order they are used.

Worker environments.

For an agentic benchmark, 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the evolution partition of the benchmark, x0x_{0} is the initial worker harness, and gg is to improve that harness under the benchmark’s evaluation rules. RℰR_{\mathcal{E}} executes a candidate harness and returns its scores, trajectories, and logs. The request uu makes execution choices part of the interface: the evolver may select tasks, set repetitions and seeds, and allocate concurrency and timeouts, subject to 𝒞ℰ\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{E}}, which fixes the benchmark rules and bounds resources. In a prescribed loop these choices are made before evolution, so the evolver only ever sees Rℰ​(x)R_{\mathcal{E}}(x) under a fixed uu. Updating prior work to use uu adaptively would require substantial domain knowledge and harness design expertise.

3.2 The Evolver Controls the Campaign

An evolver is an agent that receives this interface and runs the campaign. We instantiate it as Claude Code equipped with a self-contained evolution skill ss, a markdown file of instructions. A complete campaign is one invocation:

x⋆=Evolve⁡(s;ℰ⁡[x0])≡s⁡(g,𝒟,x0,Rℰ,𝒞ℰ).x^{\star}=\operatorname{Evolve}\!\left(s;\mathcal{E}[x_{0}]\right)\equiv s\!\left(g,\mathcal{D},x_{0},R_{\mathcal{E}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{E}}\right). (3)

The framework invokes the evolver once, provides access to RℰR_{\mathcal{E}}, and takes no further role. The evolver decides which candidate to edit, which request (x,u)(x,u) to issue, how the returned artifacts change its next decision, and when to return x⋆x^{\star}. No external loop fixes the number of executions, the organization of search, or the stopping decision. This is our operational definition of campaign autonomy: every environment execution is chosen by the evolver, and control returns to the evolver with the resulting artifacts.

Two human-designed components remain, and neither is an evolution loop. Claude Code’s own agent loop (read, act, observe) is generic tool use; it specifies no evaluation schedule, acceptance rule, or stopping criterion. The seed skill is written by hand, but it fixes only dispositions: treat the environment as the source of truth, keep all evidence, continue from the best-supported target, and use the time budget (Appendix G.1). Which tasks to evaluate, how many repetitions to buy, when to branch, and when to accept are left to the evolver.

Worker evolution.

Let ℰw​[w0]\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{w}}[w_{0}] denote a worker environment initialized with harness w0w_{0}. Worker evolution is an ordinary application of Equation 3:

w⋆=Evolve⁡(s;ℰw​[w0]).w^{\star}=\operatorname{Evolve}\left(s;\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{w}}[w_{0}]\right). (4)

Because the evolver initiates every execution, the campaign can follow the evidence: stable measurements let it move on, close comparisons justify more repetitions, and failures concentrated in part of the data can be searched there before a candidate is validated broadly. Whether a given skill organizes these choices well is a separate question, which we answer by learning the skill.

3.3 Meta-Evolution Learns the Campaign Policy

Prior meta-evolution makes the search procedure editable across outer iterations: an outer optimizer produces a new procedure for the next inner run, whose logic is then fixed while the run executes. FreeEvolve meta-evolves a different object: an evolution skill that stays active throughout the inner campaign and decides how to gather evidence and organize search as results arrive.

Because the skill is itself a text target, meta-evolution needs no new machinery. We construct a meta-environment whose editable target is an evolution skill and whose data are worker environments:

𝒟m={ℰiw​[wi]}i=1n,\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{m}}=\left\{\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{w}}_{i}[w_{i}]\right\}_{i=1}^{n}, (5)
ℰm​[s0]=(gm,𝒟m,s0,Rm,𝒞m).\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{m}}[s_{0}]=\left(g^{\mathrm{m}},\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{m}},s_{0},R_{\mathrm{m}},\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{m}}\right). (6)

A candidate skill is not scored in isolation. It is installed in the evolver for complete worker-evolution campaigns and judged through the workers and traces they produce. With ℐ⁡(u)⊆{1,…,n}\mathcal{I}(u)\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} the worker environments selected by request uu, the meta-level execution function is

Rm​(s,u)=EvaluateWorkers⁡({Evolve⁡(s;ℰiw​[wi]):i∈ℐ⁡(u)}),R_{\mathrm{m}}(s,u)=\operatorname{EvaluateWorkers}\left(\left\{\operatorname{Evolve}\left(s;\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{w}}_{i}[w_{i}]\right):i\in\mathcal{I}(u)\right\}\right), (7)

which returns the resulting workers, their evolution-partition scores, and the inner campaign records. Meta-evolution is then another application of Equation 3:

s⋆=Evolve⁡(souter;ℰm​[s0]).s^{\star}=\operatorname{Evolve}\left(s_{\mathrm{outer}};\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{m}}[s_{0}]\right). (8)

The outer evolver edits s0s_{0}, decides which inner campaigns to launch, and uses their outcomes as feedback. souters_{\mathrm{outer}} and s0s_{0} start as separate copies of the same seed skill, so editing the candidate never changes the controller. Meta-environments are excluded from 𝒟m\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{m}}, which bounds nesting at two levels. Appendix F shows the worker and meta-environments for ARC-AGI-3 side by side.

Why the environment–evolver boundary matters.

Separating environment assumptions from evolution strategy supports reuse across execution settings. On a cluster, inner campaigns finish asynchronously across nodes; an evolver tied to a single-machine execution model may leave resources idle or require changes to its control logic.

In FreeEvolve, supporting Slurm requires only an environment-specific RmslurmR_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm{slurm}}, which launches inner campaigns and returns their artifacts as they finish, and 𝒞mslurm\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm{slurm}}, which exposes node allocation and concurrency limits. The evolver, evolution skill, and Evolve\operatorname{Evolve} operation remain unchanged; the evolver adapts its campaign as jobs complete (Appendix A).

The same boundary supports skill transfer. Each setting supplies its own ℰ⁡[x0]\mathcal{E}[x_{0}], while the skill guides how the evolver uses the available capabilities and evidence. A meta-evolved skill can therefore be frozen and reused in environments with different tasks, models, or hardware, without inheriting source workers or campaign state.

4 Experiments

Our central claim is that the policy organizing agent evolution can be learned rather than fully specified by a human-designed search loop. Campaign autonomy makes adaptive decisions available, and meta-evolution learns how to use them from experience. Our experiments answer five questions. Q1: Can a learned autonomous campaign achieve strong performance without a prescribed loop? Q2: Does meta-evolution turn campaign autonomy into a stronger evolver? Q3: Does the resulting evolution skill generalize beyond its source environment and model? Q4: How does the evolver use campaign autonomy as evolution unfolds? Q5: What model capability is required to exercise campaign autonomy effectively? Appendix Table 11 summarizes the evidence for each.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate four environments spanning interactive tool use, abstract reasoning, and terminal control: τ3\tau^{3}-bench for conversational agents over unstructured knowledge (Shi et al., 2026), ARC-AGI-2 for few-shot grid transformations (Chollet et al., 2026), ARC-AGI-3 for interactive abstract-reasoning games (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026), and Terminal-Bench 2.1 for long-horizon command-line tasks (Merrill et al., 2026). We report mean task score and pass@3, except on ARC-AGI-3, where we report RHAE. Appendix Table 5 lists dataset sizes, splits, metrics, and base agents. All meta-evolution campaigns start from the same task-agnostic seed skill; Appendix G.1 gives its instructions and the campaign decisions left open to meta-evolution.

Evaluation protocol.

We measure performance on unseen tasks rather than the best score seen during search. Each method searches only on the evolution partition, with the same split and worker configuration within a benchmark, and selects its final artifact using its own rules before the held-out partition is revealed. Following the standard search protocol used in GEPA and EvoX (Agrawal et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a), we perform the search once and additionally evaluate its resulting worker on the held-out set three times, reporting the mean and standard deviation (mean ±\pm s.d.). Where defined, we also report pass@3, the fraction of tasks solved at least once across the three runs.

4.2 Learned Autonomous Campaigns Produce Strong Workers

To answer Q1, we test whether FreeEvolve can use campaign autonomy to match the performance of human-designed search loops. We compare the unmodified worker, GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025), OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), EvoX (Liu et al., 2026a), HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026b), and FreeEvolve with meta-evolution. GEPA, OpenEvolve, and EvoX follow the SkyDiscover settings (Liu et al., 2026b), and HyperAgents uses its default settings.

Autonomous and prescribed-loop methods allocate evaluations and search effort differently, making exact cost matching difficult. We therefore use Table 1 to compare their improvement frontiers under explicit stopping rules: each baseline keeps running until improvement stall for 5 iterations, while FreeEvolve receives a 24-hour meta-evolution budget, the time for different baselines are in Table 9. The comparison asks how strong a worker each method can ultimately produce under its own campaign organization.

Table 1 shows that a meta-evolved autonomous campaign produces strong workers across all four environments. FreeEvolve improves the primary held-out metric by 13.613.6 points on average and outperforms the expert-designed evolvers on three benchmarks. It also consistently matches or outperforms the meta-evolution baselines EvoX and HyperAgents, indicating the value of shifting the target of meta-evolution from a specific search loop to campaign organization.

Terminal-Bench 2.1 exposes a complementary challenge. FreeEvolve achieves the best pass@3, while its mean score trails GEPA. Terminal evaluation is particularly CPU-intensive, so a shared concurrency setting can create blocking and variable throughput. This contrast reinforces the role of the environment definition: resource availability and execution behavior should be exposed better to the evolver.

4.3 Meta-Evolution Produces a Stronger Evolver

To answer Q2, every skill starts from the same fresh worker and receives the same resource budget. The seed is the initial evolution skill; the no-data variant asks an LLM to improve that skill without observing execution results; and the meta-evolved variant is learned from completed meta-evolution. No evolved worker or campaign artifact is carried into these runs.

Figure 3 shows that the seed is already capable of improving a worker, but only modestly: it gains 0.60.6 points on average across the four mean metrics. The meta-evolved skill adds a further 6.96.9 points on average over the seed, improves every available pass@3 metric, and outperforms the no-data rewrite in every environment. Campaign autonomy makes a broad set of decisions available; these results show that meta-evolution can learn how to make those decisions effectively, reducing the need for manual expert design.

4.4 Learned Evolution Skills Transfer Across Environments and Models

To answer Q3, we test whether an evolution skill, which captures how to organize improvement rather than a particular worker, remains useful when installed elsewhere. If so, compute-intensive meta-evolution can be run once and the resulting evolver reused in new environments.

We freeze each skill learned in a separate meta-evolution campaign and install it in a fresh target environment (Table 2). Transfer is positive on most target metrics, and some transferred skills approach or exceed the in-environment result. Both single-source skills, however, reduce the Terminal-Bench 2.1 mean, and the ARC-AGI-2 skill also reduces its pass@3, suggesting a transfer boundary when the target environment, including its hardware and execution behavior, changes substantially. Joint meta-evolution on τ3\tau^{3}-bench and Terminal-Bench 2.1 yields a skill that improves every reported target metric over the seed, so exposing meta-evolution to more diverse environments can produce a more robust evolver.

We also test whether evolved worker harnesses capture task improvements rather than model-specific behavior: each method’s harness, evolved with the native Opus worker, runs unchanged with Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 (Figure 4a). Across the four non-native settings, FreeEvolve keeps an average gain of 5.35.3 points over the base harness and remains the strongest evolved harness, whereas several baseline gains on τ3\tau^{3}-bench shrink or reverse. FreeEvolve workers can therefore be evolved with a stronger model and deployed with a cheaper one without re-evolution.

Figure 4b measures how effectively each method converts its total token budget, including all evolver, evaluation, and other model calls, into a stronger evolver skill, scored by the training RHAE of the worker the skill produces. By 0.740.74B tokens, FreeEvolve has produced a skill whose worker reaches a score that no baseline attains with more than twice the total token cost.

4.5 Model Capability Supports Effective Campaign Control

Q5 asks what model capability is needed to turn campaign autonomy into held-out gains. We hold the τ3\tau^{3}-bench worker and meta-evolution setup fixed, vary only the model executing the evolver from Haiku 4.5 to Opus 4.8, and compare the resulting workers only on held-out mean and pass@3.

Table 3 reveals a clear transition. Haiku 4.5 does not improve either held-out metric; beginning with Sonnet 4.6, meta-evolution consistently improves held-out performance, with the strongest Opus models producing the best workers. Held-out improvement generally increases with newer and stronger models, although Sonnet 4.6 notably outperforms Opus 4.6. This result also identifies a limitation: producing held-out gains with FreeEvolve requires sufficient model capability. Sonnet 4.6 already demonstrates this capability; we leave a broader study of this boundary to future work.

4.6 Autonomous Campaigns Adapt Evaluation and Search

To answer Q4, we hold the learned skill and resource budget fixed while removing its control over one environment-facing decision at a time. Table 4 examines how the learned skill uses its campaign control by fixing one decision at a time. Always evaluating the full set makes the evolver wait for expensive probes, reducing the number of decisions it can make within the time budget. Fixed concurrency and the absence of timeouts leave resources occupied by slow or failed executions, using more total tokens but producing a weaker worker. The benefit is thus not one universally optimal configuration; it is the ability to reorganize evaluation as the campaign unfolds.

Qualitative campaign analysis.

The fixed-decision interventions isolate evaluation choices, but autonomy also governs the organization of search. We therefore trace one ARC-AGI-2 worker-evolution campaign using a frozen meta-evolved skill.

Figure 5 shows the evolver exercising this control online: it changes evaluation resolution, opens distinct branches, combines discoveries, and selects the final worker as evidence accumulates. These behaviors are not hard-coded stages of the framework; the evolver invokes each behavior when the campaign requires it.

To identify what meta-evolution contributes to these decisions, we compare the four meta-evolved skills with their common seed. The seed provides broad dispositions—use the available time, preserve evidence, and continue from the best worker—while leaving the organization of the campaign open. The evolved skills turn those dispositions into operational policies (Appendix D, Figure 6). Across environments, the learned rules govern task selection, evaluation allocation, and search control. They use failures to choose new probes, move from cheap tests to confirmation only when warranted, and preserve or combine changes according to accumulated evidence. Together, the intervention, execution-trace, and skill analyses answer Q4: autonomy lets the evolver request the campaign behavior it needs, while meta-evolution turns that freedom into a reusable way of organizing improvement.

5 Conclusion

Agent evolvers have automated the design of harnesses, but not the broader process that designs them. FreeEvolve automates that process too: the evolver runs its own improvement campaign in a free space, and meta-evolution learns how to run it from the outcomes. Across four environments, the automated process uses a self-controlled loop, yet matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers’ performance. Beyond autonomy, the learned process improves with experience. What it carries is a way of running an improvement campaign rather than domain knowledge. Treating the optimization process as a learnable agent capability, rather than a fixed piece of engineering, lets agent improvement advance with experience and with the models themselves.

AI Use Statement

Large language models are the object of study in this work. Every evolver, worker, simulated user, and judge is a Claude model, and the evolver agent is Claude Code. Separately, the authors used LLM assistants to edit prose, check consistency between tables and text, and write figure code. The authors designed the experiments, checked every reported number against the run artifacts, and take full responsibility for the content.

Ethics Statement

Meta-evolving an agent harness can amplify errors, consume substantial compute, and make the source of a behavioral change difficult to identify. FreeEvolve limits nesting, retains all evaluation records, fixes model capability, and separates candidate generation from acceptance. These controls improve auditability, but they do not make autonomous improvement safe for high-stakes deployment, where domain-specific oversight remains necessary.

Reproducibility Statement

Each run stores the installed environment, evaluated target, evolver instructions, execution trace, and raw evaluation results. The appendix reports the benchmark definitions, task splits, base agents, and model configurations. Additional implementation and reproducibility details are available in the anonymous code submission.

Appendix

Appendix A Implementation Details

Anonymous code.

We instantiate the evolver with Claude Code and a single instruction file, SKILL.md. One call to evolve.sh installs an environment in a fresh run directory and invokes this agent once. There is no framework-level evolution loop around that invocation. The seed skill contains only general instructions for working from evidence and leaving the strongest target behind; it does not prescribe an iteration count, branching structure, curriculum, evaluation schedule, or performance-based stopping rule.

Each installed environment realizes Equation 1 through four visible components. ENVIRONMENT.md records the goal, data, constraints, and interpretation of the returned artifacts. The file .target identifies the editable surface x0x_{0}, while run.sh implements RℰR_{\mathcal{E}}. An initially empty workspace-<env>/ stores the candidates, artifacts, and notes produced during evolution. The environment files remain fixed throughout a campaign; only the declared target is editable.

The call Rℰ​(x,u)R_{\mathcal{E}}(x,u) is implemented in place. The evolver installs candidate xx at the path declared by .target and supplies uu through the arguments of run.sh. Each call records its measurements and traces in an artifact directory. Evaluation always reads the declared edit surface, ensuring that the candidate under evaluation is the candidate being evolved.

The run directory is the complete interface between environment and evolver. It is self-contained, records the skill and model used for the run, and preserves the evaluation artifacts produced during the campaign. The evolver may invoke run.sh in any order or configuration, launch independent branches, and decide when enough evidence has been collected. The framework enforces the environment boundary, but contributes no search schedule.

The meta-environment uses exactly the same layout. Its declared target is a candidate SKILL.md, and its run.sh launches that skill as the evolver in a fresh worker environment. A meta-level execution returns the complete inner run directory, including the worker produced, its evaluations, and the inner trace, rather than reducing the campaign to a fixed scalar. The outer evolver chooses which worker environment to launch and how many inner runs to collect. Meta-environments are excluded from the inner environment catalogue, bounding execution to the two levels described above.

Hardware and campaign budgets.

Standalone worker-evolution runs receive a 12-hour wall-clock budget on one 128-CPU machine. The environment permits at most 24 concurrent task attempts, regardless of how the evolver divides them among evaluation calls.

Meta-evolution receives a 24-hour outer-campaign budget on a Slurm cluster with five worker nodes. The meta-environment submits each requested inner campaign as an independent one-node Slurm job, and 𝒞m\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{m}} permits at most five inner campaigns to run simultaneously. We impose no separate wall-clock limit on an inner evolver within meta-evolution: deciding how many inner campaigns to launch, how long to let them run, and how to coordinate asynchronous completions is part of the meta-evolver’s campaign control.

Appendix B Dataset Details

τ3\tau^{3}-bench.

We use the banking_knowledge domain. Each task is a tool-mediated conversation with a simulated customer. The agent must retrieve the relevant bank policy, take any required actions, and communicate the correct resolution. The grader assigns a binary reward after the conversation. The full domain contains 97 tasks; our fixed split places 68 tasks in the evolution partition and 29 in the held-out partition.

ARC-AGI-2.

ARC-AGI-2 consists of few-shot visual reasoning tasks represented as input–output grid transformations (Chollet et al., 2026). A solver must infer the latent transformation from the demonstrations and apply it to a new input. We use 56 tasks for evolution and a disjoint set of 111 held-out tasks. Meta-evolution may use only the 56-task evolution partition. We report task accuracy on the held-out partition.

ARC-AGI-3.

ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive abstract-reasoning games (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026). We use 17 games for evolution and reserve 8 disjoint games for held-out evaluation. The agent interacts with each game through the declared environment interface, while the game definitions and evaluator remain fixed. We report Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE). Each completed level receives the squared ratio of human-baseline actions to agent actions, subject to the benchmark’s cap for faster-than-human play; uncompleted levels receive zero. Level scores are linearly weighted so later levels count more, each game is capped by the weighted fraction of levels completed, and RHAE averages the resulting game scores. We report it as a percentage, with higher values indicating more complete and action-efficient play.

Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Terminal-Bench 2.1 contains realistic command-line tasks executed in isolated containers (Merrill et al., 2026). Tasks include software debugging, systems configuration, security, data processing, and scientific workflows. Each task provides a problem statement and a test suite that verifies the final container state. We report results on 61 held-out tasks. We report mean and pass@3.

All task partitions are created before meta-evolution. Neither the worker-level nor the meta-level evolver may access the held-out partition. The same split is used for all compared evolver generations within a benchmark. To ensure evolver do not break out of the working directory to find held-out set, we perform keyword search of held-out data IDs over the run directory. The evolvers consistently stay within the established run directory without attempting to hack held-out data.

Appendix C Configuration Details

Model matching.

Unless otherwise stated, the worker, worker-level evolver, and outer meta-evolver use the same Claude model within an environment. The model-capability experiment is the explicit exception. This design evaluates self-improvement without introducing a stronger teacher model.

Each environment is installed into a fresh run directory containing its ENVIRONMENT.md, evaluator, declared edit surface, and an empty workspace. The evolver runs from that directory. It may modify the declared target and write to its workspace; it cannot edit the environment or redirect the evaluator to another target.

τ3\tau^{3}-bench configuration.

The base worker is the vendored τ3\tau^{3} customer-service agent. The agent, simulated user, and judge each use bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8. The agent’s reasoning effort is fixed to medium. The editable surface includes the agent prompt, tool-use loop, response parsing, retry behavior, and termination logic; changing the model, reasoning capability, task data, tools, policy, or grader is out of scope.

ARC-AGI-2 configuration.

The base worker is an ARC-AGI-2 solver backed by Claude 4.7 Opus. The model and inference configuration are held fixed across the base, seed-evolver, and meta-evolved conditions. The evolver may modify the solver harness and its search procedure, but not the task grids, evolution/held-out split, or correctness evaluator. Each reported worker is produced from the same base solver rather than inherited from the preceding condition.

ARC-AGI-3 configuration.

The base worker is an ARC-AGI-3 agent backed by Claude Opus 5. The model, reasoning configuration, game definitions, and evaluator are fixed across conditions. The evolver may modify the declared agent harness and search procedure but may not modify the games or their scoring implementation.

Terminal-Bench 2.1 configuration.

The base worker is the unmodified deep agent. It uses bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-4-8 with temperature 1.0. The editable surface includes the agent control loop, prompts, response parsers, and terminal-session handling. Container definitions, task statements, test suites, and verifier code remain fixed.

Interpretation.

The end-to-end results show that evolver-controlled campaigns improve the complete system across all four environments. Fresh-worker tests isolate improvement stored in the evolution skill, while cross-environment evaluation tests whether that improvement transfers. The fixed-uu study isolates several environment-facing decisions, and the campaign trace shows that the evolver also adapts search structure.

Appendix E Additional Related Work

Broader harness evolution and self-improvement.

ADAS and AFlow search over coded agent designs and workflows (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Continual Harness adapts prompts, tools, skills, and memory during interaction (Karten et al., 2026); Life-Harness, Living-Harness, and SkillOpt-Lite retain reusable runtime or procedural improvements (Xu et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026); and AutoHarness and Agentic Harness Engineering search over code and workflow surfaces (Lou et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). AlphaEvolve provides a general evolutionary coding system with a prescribed evaluation loop (Novikov et al., 2025). Self-improving systems have also widened the improver’s edit surface: PromptBreeder evolves mutation prompts (Fernando et al., 2024); STOP applies a program improver to its own source (Zelikman et al., 2024); and Gödel Agent, the Darwin Gödel Machine, and SICA let coding agents modify their own code (Yin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025). Bilevel Autoresearch and Meta Context Engineering improve mechanisms or skills using downstream outcomes (Qu and Lu, 2026; Ye et al., 2026). Autonomous research agents such as AIDE choose their own experiments while optimizing a task artifact (Jiang et al., 2025); FreeEvolve instead learns the reusable skill that organizes future improvement campaigns.

Transferring products and improvement procedures.

HarnessCompass, Meta-Harness, Agentic Harness Engineering, and the Darwin Gödel Machine evaluate whether final evolved harnesses or agents transfer to new tasks or models (Zhang et al., 2026c; Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). TTHE instead adapts executable harnesses on the evaluation tasks themselves (Nie et al., 2026). These studies primarily transfer the product of improvement. STOP transfers an evolved program improver across small algorithmic tasks (Zelikman et al., 2024). HyperAgents transfers meta-level improvement mechanisms, and AIDE2 evaluates an evolved optimizer beyond the tasks that produced it (Zhang et al., 2026b; Srikanth et al., 2026). FreeEvolve freezes the meta-evolved evolution skill before it sees the target environment and installs it in an evolver operating on a fresh worker. The target supplies its own data, model, execution function, and resource constraints; no source worker, search branch, or execution artifact is retained. This tests whether the learned improvement process itself generalizes, rather than only whether its previously evolved product does.

Appendix F Concrete Example for Worker and Meta-Evolver Environments

For both worker and meta-evolver environments, ENVIRONMENT.md specifies the goal, editable target, available data, resource limits, and edit constraints. The worker environment and top-level meta-environment each provide their own file. Table 12 compares the two contracts for ARC-AGI-3.

What happens in one concrete meta-evaluation.

The outer evolver first edits target/SKILL.md, then invokes run.sh with --inner-env arc_agi_3. The meta-environment creates a fresh run containing the ARC-AGI-3 worker contract and installs the candidate evolution skill in the inner evolver. That evolver edits agent/arc3_agent/, chooses games and repetitions, and evaluates worker versions using Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE). The complete inner run—worker versions, scores, traces, costs, and its nominated best worker—returns as evidence to the outer evolver, which uses it to revise the skill.

The key distinction.

At the worker level, a candidate is an agent and an evaluation is a set of game plays. At the meta-level, a candidate is an evolution policy and an evaluation is an entire worker-evolution trajectory. The worker environment ranks matched agents with a benchmark metric; the meta-evolver judges both the workers and the quality and cost of the process that produced them. The interface is shared, but the target, evaluation unit, and acceptance decision are not.

Appendix G Prompts

G.1 Canonical Seed Evolution Skill

The evolver is stored as a versioned SKILL.md file. Every reported meta-evolution lineage starts from the same canonical seed. The seed is task-agnostic but not has instruction on how to interact with environement and be punctual with the time budget so we can control the experiments. The following excerpts preserve its operative language while omitting repeated persistence reminders.

We observe that the evolver does not necessarily put the harness performing the best in the best folder. It has its own way to decide the delivered harness by including the total number of evaluation, paired comparison, etc, into consideration, showing that the evolver does more than maximizing benchmark scores.

G.2 Meta-Evolved Instruction

The meta-evolved version adds a more detailed experimental procedure. It instructs the learner to establish a baseline, diagnose failed trajectories, test different types of changes, account for noisy measurements, retain candidate versions, and restore the best-supported target before finishing.
